newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu undeterred by U.S., world criticism.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu undeterred by U.S., world criticism.

text.p: Israel's leader Benjamin Netanyahu shrugged off criticism by U.S. President Bill Clinton on Tuesday, vowing to start work within days on a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

But Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, on a visit to Washington, said he had no alternative to pursuing peace talks with Netanyahu despite last week's decision to build 6,500 homes for Jews at Jabal Abu Ghneim, called Har Homa by Israel.
Netanyahu, speaking on Israeli Army Radio, said bulldozers would begin to move in two weeks on the pine-covered Jerusalem hill at the centre of an international controversy.
"From the standpoint of the survey work it's only a few days," the Israeli prime minister said. "We are determined to go on building in Jerusalem."
Clinton sided with Arafat at a White House meeting on Monday, saying Netanyahu's plan to build the homes in the city that will be subject to future Israel-PLO negotiation would fuel "mistrust".
"There was nothing new in what he (Clinton) said," Netanyahu told the radio. "The Americans understand our policy well."
Israel captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war and annexed it, a move not recognised internationally, to claim all the city as its capital.

The PLO, which is supposed to negotiate the city's fate with Israel in talks due to end in 1999, sees construction at Jabal Abu Ghneim as an attempt to block its demand East Jerusalem become capital of a Palestinian state.
A U.N. Security Council debate scheduled to begin on Tuesday on the Israeli housing project was postponed until Wednesday at the request of the United States.

"We felt that a short delay would be helpful and we look forward tomorrow to a briefing by Chairman Arafat in the morning and then a discussion of the settlements issue in the afternoon," U.S. ambassador Bill Richardson said in New York.
At a Washington news conference on Tuesday, Arafat again bitterly denounced the Israeli decision, calling it an illegal move that created a "real challenge" to the peace process.
Nevertheless, Arafat said: "It is our duty and our job and our target to carry on with the peace process...This is our strategic target."
Israeli moves in Jerusalem sparked violence in September. Sixty-one Arabs and 15 Israeli soldiers died in gunbattles after Netanyahu opened a tourist tunnel entrance near Islamic shrines.
In Washington, Arafat said he considered Netanyahu his peace "partner" just as previous Labour prime ministers were.

"I have to respect what the Israelis have elected...We are making the peace with the Israeli people. He is now my partner, as (Yitzhak) Rabin was my partner, as Shimon Peres was my partner, now my partner is Mr Netanyahu," Arafat said.
A defiant Netanyahu said Israelis were united in viewing Jerusalem as their capital.

"It could be the world doesn't agree to our sovereignty in Jerusalem...I don't intend to be influenced by opposition of one kind or another," he said in the radio interview, citing legal and technical reasons for the delay in breaking ground.
Netanyahu was due to hear more criticism of the Jerusalem project when he meets Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Wednesday in Cairo.

The Israeli leader said he would convene a cabinet meeting this week to discuss carrying out the next withdrawal of Israeli troops from parts of the West Bank as agreed with the PLO in January. The redeployment is due to take place by Friday.
"I imagine we will begin carrying it out immediately after a decision will be taken," Netanyahu told Israel Radio.
Later in the day, Netanyahu met French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette to discuss Middle East peace moves.

"During the meeting (with de Charette), the prime minister made clear the importance of Jerusalem as the capital of Israel and pointed out that the government is looking out for Jews and Arabs in Jerusalem," Netanyahu's spokesman said.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel arrives in Israel on Wednesday.

In a bid to blunt criticism of the building project, Israel has said it would allow another 3,000 homes for Arabs in East Jerusalem. Peace activists dismissed the announcement as a public relations ploy unlikely to be carried out.
